## CUDA element loops and per-thread workspaces (`gpu_mem_kernel`) {#sec-ch12-kernels}

### Summary

kintera's CUDA kernels give each grid cell one GPU thread. That thread runs the whole per-cell solver: a small
dense linear solve, or an active-set iteration. Such a solver needs scratch arrays whose size depends on the number
of species and reactions. Each thread therefore gets its own slice of the block's shared memory, sized before the
launch. The block shrinks when the slices of a full block do not fit the device's shared-memory limit. The launch
fails when one slice alone does not fit.

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
**Purpose.** Run a per-cell solver as one CUDA thread per cell, with scratch in shared memory.

**Data.** Per-cell inputs and outputs through a tensor iterator; scratch bytes per thread.

**Placement.** The CUDA driver of each dispatch stub (@sec-ch12-dispatch).

**Activation.** Always, on CUDA inputs.

**Guarantee / limits.** At most 32 threads per block; the scratch of one cell must fit the per-block limit.

**Evidence.** See the Tests layer below.
:::

Local symbols: $n_{\mathrm{s}}$ the number of species, $b$ the scratch bytes of one cell, $M$ the device's largest
per-block dynamic shared memory [bytes] and $N_{\mathrm{thr}}$ the threads per block.

### Derivation

The launcher `gpu_mem_kernel` ({{< code src/loops.cuh gpu_mem_kernel >}}) picks the block size from the scratch size
of one cell:

$$
N_{\mathrm{thr}} = \min\left(N_{\max},\ \max\left(1,\ \left\lfloor M / b \right\rfloor\right)\right)
$$ {#eq-ch12-kernels-threads}

@eq-ch12-kernels-threads is computed in `gpu_mem_kernel` ({{< code src/loops.cuh gpu_mem_kernel >}}),
and it stops with an error when $N_{\mathrm{thr}}\,b > M$, which happens exactly when $b > M$. Both directions
follow from the formula. If $b \le M$ then $\lfloor M/b \rfloor \ge 1$, so $N_{\mathrm{thr}} \le \lfloor M/b \rfloor$
and $N_{\mathrm{thr}}\,b \le M$: no error. If $b > M$ then $\lfloor M/b \rfloor = 0$, the inner $\max$ raises it to
1, and the requested $1 \cdot b$ already exceeds $M$.

Here $N_{\max}$ is the launcher's `Threads` template parameter, not a property of the hardware. It is **32 at every
call site** at the code pin: the implicit kinetics step ({{< code src/kinetics/evolve_implicit_dispatch.cu
call_evolve_implicit_cuda >}}) and the two saturation-adjustment drivers
({{< code src/thermo/thermo_dispatch.cu call_equilibrate_tp_cuda >}} and `call_equilibrate_uv_cuda`) all instantiate
`gpu_mem_kernel<32, ...>`, so $N_{\max} = 32$ throughout this chapter. A per-cell function that needs no scratch
passes `work_size` $=0$; the launcher then skips the division and keeps the full $N_{\max}$, and
@eq-ch12-kernels-threads, which divides by $b$, does not apply.

$M$ comes from `get_max_dynamic_shared_memory` ({{< code src/loops.cuh get_max_dynamic_shared_memory >}}), cached
once per device. It starts from the ordinary per-block limit `sharedMemPerBlock` and raises it to the opt-in limit,
which it reads through the CUDA device attribute `cudaDevAttrMaxSharedMemoryPerBlockOptin`. It falls back to the
device property `sharedMemPerBlockOptin` only when that query fails, and never lets either value *lower* the ordinary
limit. The code's comment gives the reason: some runtimes report the property as 1, and taking it at face value would
cap every block at a single byte.

**Scratch bytes of the implicit step.** Two size functions contribute, and it matters which gives what:

| source | matrices $n_{\mathrm{s}}\times n_{\mathrm{s}}$ | vectors of length $n_{\mathrm{s}}$ |
|---|---|---|
| `evolve_implicit_space` ({{< code src/kinetics/evolve_implicit_impl.h evolve_implicit_space >}}) | 2: `A`, `Alu` | 2: `sr`, `x` |
| `psolve_space`, the pseudo-inverse fallback ({{< code src/utils/alloc.h psolve_space >}}) | 2: `ATA`, `V` | 4: `eval`, `vi`, `Avi`, `b0` |
| total | 4 | 6 |

: Scratch allocations of the per-cell implicit step. {#tbl-ch12-kernels-implicit-parts}

Each allocation is rounded up on its own to a multiple of 8 bytes by `pool_allocation_bytes`
({{< code src/utils/alloc.h pool_allocation_bytes >}}), matching the 8-byte alignment of the shared-memory block.
Writing $\lceil x \rceil_8$ for that rounding and $s$ for the bytes of one entry, the scratch of one cell is

$$
b(n_{\mathrm{s}}, s) = 4\,\big\lceil s\,n_{\mathrm{s}}^2 \big\rceil_8 + 6\,\big\lceil s\,n_{\mathrm{s}} \big\rceil_8 .
$$ {#eq-ch12-kernels-implicit-bytes}

@eq-ch12-kernels-implicit-bytes is the sum of the allocations of `evolve_implicit_space`
({{< code src/kinetics/evolve_implicit_impl.h evolve_implicit_space >}}). In double precision $s = 8$, every term is already a multiple of 8, the rounding does nothing, and

$$
b(n_{\mathrm{s}}, 8) = 4 \cdot 8\,n_{\mathrm{s}}^2 + 6 \cdot 8\,n_{\mathrm{s}}
 = 32\,n_{\mathrm{s}}^2 + 48\,n_{\mathrm{s}} .
$$ {#eq-ch12-kernels-implicit-bytes-double}

That is the value `evolve_implicit_space`
({{< code src/kinetics/evolve_implicit_impl.h evolve_implicit_space >}}) returns for `double`.
In single precision $s = 4$ the rounding is not idle, and $b$ is **not** $16\,n_{\mathrm{s}}^2 + 24\,n_{\mathrm{s}}$.
A term $4n_{\mathrm{s}}$ or $4n_{\mathrm{s}}^2$ is a multiple of 8 only when $n_{\mathrm{s}}$, respectively
$n_{\mathrm{s}}^2$, is even, so each odd-sized allocation is padded by 4 bytes. At $n_{\mathrm{s}} = 3$, for example,
@eq-ch12-kernels-implicit-bytes gives $4 \cdot 40 + 6 \cdot 16 = 256$ bytes against the 216 the unrounded expression
would give. Single precision is not a side case: every C++ test built on `DeviceTest` runs in both precisions
(Tests layer), so the block-size bounds below have to be read with the precision stated.

On a device with $M = 49152$ bytes, in double precision, @eq-ch12-kernels-threads and
@eq-ch12-kernels-implicit-bytes-double give $N_{\mathrm{thr}} = 32$ for $n_{\mathrm{s}} \le 6$, because
$32 \cdot 36 + 48 \cdot 6 = 1440 \le 49152/32 = 1536$ while $n_{\mathrm{s}} = 7$ gives 1904 and so 25 threads. They
give a launch error for $n_{\mathrm{s}} \ge 39$, because $32 \cdot 39^2 + 48 \cdot 39 = 50544 > 49152$ while
$n_{\mathrm{s}} = 38$ gives 48032. `check_ch12_twins.py` recomputes both from the code's own allocation list: line g
reads "implicit-step scratch from the size function equals 32 ns^2 + 48 ns for ns = 1..59 PASS", and line h reads
"M=49152: threads ns=6 32, ns=7 25; launch error ns=38 False, ns=39 True (report: 32 up to 6, error from 39)
PASS".[^ch12-kernels-check] $M = 49152$ is a value of one device generation, not a constant: the check fixes it to
compare with this text, and a device with a larger opt-in limit moves both bounds. Neither the shrunken block nor
the launch error has been run on a GPU (Limits).

### Numerical method

Each thread of `gpu_mem_kernel` ({{< code src/loops.cuh gpu_mem_kernel >}}) works as follows:

1. It computes the offsets of its cell's inputs and outputs from the tensor iterator.
2. It takes the slice of shared memory at `threadIdx.x` times the per-cell scratch size.
3. It calls the per-cell function with that slice. The per-cell function allocates its arrays from the slice with
   the bump allocator `pmalloc` ({{< code src/utils/alloc.h pmalloc >}}), and it releases them all at once by
   resetting the pointer with `pool_rewind` ({{< code src/utils/alloc.h pool_rewind >}}).

When a full block needs more than the ordinary per-block limit, the launcher raises the kernel's dynamic
shared-memory attribute once per device before the first launch.

### Tests

| test (ctest name) | what it asserts | tolerance | where the tolerance comes from |
|---|---|---|---|
| `test_cuda_workspace.py` | TP and UV saturation adjustment with shared-memory scratch, CUDA against CPU | `rtol=1e-10`, `atol=1e-14` | not stated in the test |
| `test_alloc_space.release` | that three per-cell solvers stay *inside* their declared budget; not the budget's value | exact (a guard byte) | the pool guard |
| `test_kinetics` | the implicit step on CUDA | exact status | the return code |

: Tests of the CUDA element loops. {#tbl-ch12-kernels-tests}

All three pass in a CUDA build on a compute capability 6.1 GPU.[^ch12-kernels-run] On that GPU the per-block limit
$M$ is 49152 bytes, and the opt-in limit is the same, so @eq-ch12-kernels-threads applies with
$M = 49152$.[^ch12-kernels-smem] No test covers a species count large enough to shrink the block or to reach the
launch error.

**What `test_alloc_space` does and does not cover.** It is easy to read its name as a check of
@eq-ch12-kernels-implicit-bytes; it is not. It holds three typed cases, `leastsq_kkt_stays_in_budget`,
`leastsq_kkt_feasible_origin_stays_in_budget` and `equilibrate_uv_stays_in_budget`, each of which runs the solver
on a poisoned pool and asserts that a guard byte past the declared size is still intact. That is a containment
statement: the solver does not write beyond what its size function promised. It does not assert that the size
function returns the value this chapter derives, it does not touch `evolve_implicit_space` at all, and it is a plain
typed test rather than a `DeviceTest`, so it runs on the host only and never checks a budget on CUDA. The equality
in @eq-ch12-kernels-implicit-bytes-double is instead checked by `check_ch12_twins.py` line g, from the code's own
allocation list, without a GPU.[^ch12-kernels-check] The alignment rule of @eq-ch12-kernels-implicit-bytes in single
precision is checked by neither (Limits).

### Limits

::: {.callout-warning title="Limits"}
- **Large species counts on small shared memory (hypothesis, not measured).** By
  @eq-ch12-kernels-implicit-bytes-double, the implicit step on a 49152-byte device runs fewer than 32 threads per
  block for more than 6 species and cannot launch for 39 species or more, in double precision. Both bounds are
  arithmetic on the code, reproduced by `check_ch12_twins.py` line h; neither the slowdown nor the launch error has
  been run on a GPU. Both move on a device with a larger opt-in limit.
- **The single-precision scratch size is derived but unchecked.** @eq-ch12-kernels-implicit-bytes carries the
  rounding for any entry size, but `check_ch12_twins.py` evaluates its helper only at $s = 8$ (line g, "ns = 1..59"),
  so the 4-byte padding at odd $n_{\mathrm{s}}$, and the block-size bounds that follow from it in single precision,
  are not covered by any committed check.
:::

- The comment in `gpu_mem_kernel` names a 64 KiB limit for one GPU generation. The limit is read from the device
  at run time, and 49152 bytes is measured on compute capability 6.1.
- `test_alloc_space` is a containment test on the host, not a size equality and not a CUDA test (Tests layer).
- TODO: the scratch formulas of the saturation-adjustment solvers, and the same bounds for them.
  `check_ch12_twins.py` lines f-equilibrate_tp and f-equilibrate_uv already show that their size functions list 8 and
  10 allocations matching the `pmalloc` sequences in order, which is the input such a derivation needs.
